content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 22: Security Logging, Monitoring, and Incident Response. It builds practical understanding of Monitoring and Alerting with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Monitoring and Alerting turns a security intention into evidence, an operational owner, and a repeatable control. Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Monitoring and Alerting can be understood through this sequence: Capture security event → Redact sensitive values → Correlate signals → Respond + retest. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 163.1 Failed-login patterns; 163.2 Repeated authorization failures; 163.3 Unusual API usage and resource consumption; 163.4 Suspicious configuration changes; 163.5 Alert quality and false-positive reduction; 163.6 Monitoring coverage and service health. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Monitoring and Alerting
content_blocks.expected_output: A structured security event provides correlation and outcome context without storing a password, session token, or raw sensitive payload.
content_blocks.run_instructions: All values are synthetic. Avoid logging credentials, access tokens, payment data, or unnecessary personal information; apply retention and access controls to logs.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Monitoring and Alerting”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Monitoring and Alerting in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Monitoring and Alerting is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
